doc.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020

title: Basie, Lester Young and Miles Davis: music bigger than the notes
summary: Harris calls Basie and Young his heroes, says their music came from the community outward, and that Miles represented black pride; Blackout's album is built on personal relationships with composers.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I’m glad you said that, because it seems there is so much to reflect in the arts now, maybe just so many things that are happening all at the same time, yet over my shoulder are Lester Young and Count Basie, and incredible to think that their music at the time was probably eighty years ago. And do you feel that what they were doing carried as much significance to the community as what you are doing?

Well that’s a tough question because those are my heroes so I’m doing what I can to gain a seat next to them even if it’s like twenty levels down. I just want to be as close to those icons as possible. But what I will say is, as we look at the development of our art form in this country, and we look at the effect of institutionalization on the art form. So when you’re looking at Count Basie or Lester Young, this is before jazz was inside of conservatories and music programs. So the music was really primarily being generated from the community outward. So when you think about it, Count Basie, I don’t think that there was much separation between his community here in Newark, and he’s from Red Bank originally but Newark, New Jersey is where he spent a lot of time in addition to Kansas City, he was in the neighborhood with the people, uplifting people. So I think there was a deep sense of connection. And even when I think about Miles Davis and obviously he’s a genius as an artist, but I think the social strength that we were experiencing as a nation in the late 60s and 70s, especially as an African-American, I think we were in a space where we needed to be able to stand up, just like James Brown said, “Say it loud/I’m black and I’m proud.” And I think Miles Davis represented that, in all his intelligence, all of his elegance, all of his swagger. Like I’m not going to change who I am. I know that I’m beautiful and I’m going to lead with that. So their function in society was bigger than the notes. They really represented the communities from which they arose.
Yeah. “Bigger than the notes” I like that.

We try to do the same thing of course. And when I think about the music that we’re creating I’m never picking a random song from the past because it sounds good to me. Everything on our current album is there because I had a real life experience with the composer where I’ve spent time with them and they’ve had some impact in my life. This album is about my family, my wife, it’s about my brothers and sisters and what’s happening right now.
